text:
A little over a year ago I decided to stick my toe in the HiRes Digital Audio pool. I didn‚Äôt have a boat load of Benjamin‚Äôs to sink into the endeavor but I did get the best my budget could afford. I got the HiBy R6 DAP and two IEM‚Äôs to go with it. The TinAudio T2‚Äôs and the BGVP DMG‚ÄôS. Both are outstanding IEM‚Äôs but I had been hearing a lot of buzz about the hybrid electrostatic/DD Tin P1‚Äôs and was seriously considering going that way. The T2‚Äôs were a good buy and the P1‚Äôs were getting great reviews from uToobers I trust. Then about a month ago these BQEYZ Spring 1‚Äôs hit the market and the buzz shifted. I decided to give them a spin. If they weren‚Äôt a big enough improvement over the BGVP‚Äôs I could always return ‚Äòem. Well they ain‚Äôt going anywhere. The advances in personal audio over the course of the last year have been remarkable. I‚Äôm not a big fan of Chinese stuff but they are getting a solid reputation for two of the markets I dabble in, HiRes Audio and folding knives. As for these Spring 1‚Äôs they f*ing rock. Amazing soundstage, crisp punchy bass, outstanding mids and perfectly fine highs (I say perfectly fine because I have tinnitus and my hearing craps out at about 15kHz). Every instrument has its place and is distinct. The first thing I listened to was Pink Floyd Meddle and it nearly brought tears to my eyes. For an investment of just under $200 (I got the 16 core silver cable upgrade, although the stock one is perfectly adequate) you really can‚Äôt go wrong. Can‚Äôt wait for next year.

I did have the opportunity to compare these with the Shuoer Tape hybrid IEM‚Äôs and it only took me about t minutes to box up the Tape‚Äôs and return them. text:
The Rosewill RX304 USB HDD enclosure that I received works, but the tray design is really quite awful. I'm not going to return it, but the next time I buy a 3.5 inch HDD USB enclosure I will look elsewhere.

I own both the Thermaltake Max 5G (USB3) & Max 4 (USB2) HDD enclosures. I also have worked with one of the Sabrent "fan-ed" USB HDD enclosures. I cannot remember if it was USB 2 or 3.

The Sabrent enclosure was pretty good, other than the fact that the enclosure box "slid around" in its stand (the part that contacts the table/shelf).

The Thermaltake enclosures are the best and most everything about them is top notch. Unfortunately, Thermaltake no longer manufactures this sort of enclosure. They do still make BlacX USB docks. Those are docks, not enclosures.

Rosewill RX304 USB HDD enclosure
------------------------------------------

First come the complaints.

Rosewill provided incorrect HDD screws/bolts. When working with PCs there are normally only 2 types of screws/bolts = coarse thread and fine thread. HDDs take coarse thread screws. The 4 screws the Rosewill provided looked like coarse thread screws, but they wouldn't go into my HDDs more then a couple of turns. I threw them out and used my own screws.

At this point I have tried 3 different 3.5 inch HDDs with the Rosewill RX304 enclosure and none of the HDDs were able to become fully seated within the HDD tray. By fully seated I mean that all 4 HDD screw holes line up with the screw holes of the HDD tray. I was never able to get more than 2 screws in. I used WD and Seagate HDDs.

But before trying to align the screw holes you have to get the HDD into the tray in the 1st place. THIS IS VERY DIFFICULT TO DO because the tray (at the top) is ever so slightly narrower then the HDD that is going into it. WhiskeyTangoFoxtrot??? I guess that I should try bending the tray wall outwards to make it permanently wider. As a buyer I'm supposed to doing this kind of BS maneuver? This is a very bad joke ... and it is on me. If I bend the tray wall outwards will I break something?

The mechanical engineer that designed this tray is going to hell when they die.

OK. So now the HDD is in the tray (with only 2 screws) and the SATA cables are attached. The SATA cable attachments are a whole other mediocre story, but they can be made to work, so we will continue.

One (or more) reviewer/s suggested that the air passage that remains after seating the HDD is not wide enough for decent air flow to the fan and then out of the case. I could be wrong, but I suspect that there is is just enough space for reasonable air flow.

Second comes the reasonably good part.

Once the HDD is in the tray and the tray (plus interface board) is reinserted into the enclosure box you can put the end on and attach it with 2 screws. This part of the procedure is OK, but nowhere near top quality. There is an internal rail inside the enclosure box that aligns the HDD/tray/interface board within said box. But, there are only 2 "keys" in the frame that go into the rail, so the HDD tray assembly is sorta slip/sliding around in the box until you get it fully inserted, at which time the end edge of the enclosure box mates up with an internal channel in the plastic front end.

So now we have the box fully assembled, and we put it in its stand (4 rubber "nubs" keep the box from slipping around, nice). We then cable up the enclosure's power and connect the USB 3 to a computer.

Once all of the above is done you get pretty good performance. On a 2 TB HDD I was able to read the outside tracks at 200 MB/sec. That's the same performance that I get with that HDD inside a computer cabled directly to the mobo. The USB 3 interface worked well for me.

On a slightly down note the program HDDScan could not read the SMART values  through the interface board of the Rosewill RX304, but was able to read the SMART values through the interface board of a 2.5 inch Mediasonic USB 3 enclosure that I also own. Other programs may well be able to "penetrate" this USB interface to get SMART data ... who knows.

As I said at the start the Rosewill RX304 is OK, but I won't be buying any more of these units.
title: It works, but TERRIBLE tray design

text:
I have a steel roof home, which hinders the FM reception on my HD Radio receiver. Up until now I'd been piggy backing my reception off my flat Mohu TV window antenna with an amplifier. Note this window does not face the broadcast towers. But last week I realized my antenna had an FM trap, so I was excited try a switch to the Terk.

Unfortunately, the Terk doesn't perform as well as the Mohu, even using the amplifier and experimenting with different placements. However, I was motivated to revisit my old  dipole wire antenna and use it with the amp. To my surprise, when experimenting with positioning, the dipole performed better than either of the newer antennas. I'd say about 1-2 bars better on my 5 bar meter, depending on which antenna I'm using, and the station.

text:
When you order a $400 pair of headphones the last thing that you expect is for the manufacturer to take a bunch of shortcuts on quality, but this high-end pair of Technics headphones seem to be full of compromises and it almost seems like the company put more effort into marketing and packaging than it did in the final product.

The biggest letdown with this product is it's construction. It's almost entirely made of plastic, which is something that you might expect from a pair of $35 Bluetooth headphones, but not ones that sell for nearly $400. Obviously, the headphone is not going to be covered under warranty if the plastic construction breaks, and since it is mostly plastic, that is what is most likely to break first.

The other big compromises are the lack of the latest in Bluetooth technology, which is Bluetooth 5.0. There are plenty of headphones selling for far under $100 that use Bluetooth 5.0. Why not these? Charging is another issue. Rather than a fast charging USB-C connection or a convenient wireless charging connection there is a cheap and antiquated Micro-USB charger input. Again, fine for a cheap pair of headphones, but when you are talking about $400 headphones you expect MUCH better. The ear pads are also less comfortable than I would expect in this price class. They aren't horrible, but do not have the ultra soft, leather-like feel to them that you expect in high-end headphones.

On to the good things about these headphones... The packaging is really nice. If only the product was designed as well as the packing I would be so happy with this product. Bluetooth connectivity is flawless, but most $20 Bluetooth products can say the same. The ANC feature is both flexible and powerful. They do a great job at blocking out outside noise without affecting audio quality. From my limited experience with ANC headphones, these are the best I have tried thus far.

The audio quality is also quite impressive for a Bluetooth device. While it does not produce he best sound I have ever heard from a pair of corded headphones they are on par with the best Bluetooth headphones I have used. I would hesitate to say that they are THE best sounding Bluetooth headphones I have used though.

While these are "nice" Bluetooth headphones they come nowhere near what I would expect from something in this price class. They are about on par with what you would expect for a pair of Bluetooth headphones selling in the $180-$200 range, but that's it. The lack of latest features and the use of plastic throughout it's construction really rubs me the wrong way. If these sold at half of their current price I might give them a four star review. I think that I am being generous at giving them the three stars that they are getting though.
title: Mid-Range Quality At A High-End Price

This outlet strip works o.k. Just don't take the description of the product too seriously. For one thing, it claims to provide a total of 2.4 Amps to each of it's 4 charging ports, but provides a total of only 4.2 Amps. Even a third grader can tell you that 2.4 x 4 is more than 4.2. So, the total amount of Amps per port is only about half of what is claimed. So, you can pretty much forget fast charging any of your devices if you have more than 3 items charging at the same time.

I'm not sure about the claim of the 2 AC outlets having "supper wide space". Maybe it means that you get more space while eating dinner? It also claims to feature "4 smart Micro USB ports".  Nope. They are just regular sized USB ports, not micro, which would make no sense anyway.

Other than that, this "power strip", as they call it, is pretty unremarkable. It is missing a great number of functions that you would expect, even in it's price range. Some of the features that it does NOT include are: NO surge protection or line filtering, NO reset switch, NO on/off switch, No ability for the plug to swivel positions, NO LED to show if the charger outlets are working, NO clamps along the side of the unit to coil the cord around. NO warranty beyond 30 days and NO company contact information.

So, it's basically just a cheaply constructed Chinese product with only 2 AC outlets and maybe 2 outlets that will quick charge your phone at the same time. Nothing too exciting here.

text:
Caveats:  Routers are always hit or miss and if you read any review you will see (much like other products I guess) the 1 or 2 stars reviews complaining about having to reset the router, weak signal and so on.  Every Netgear or TP-Link or Linksys routers I have had, they do great for a while and for some reason they just need an occasional and then a frequent reset till you decide it's time to upgrade.  So, long term jury is out on this one much like other routers.  Having used this in my house for under 24 hours, this router is performing as it should.  I would recommend it based on my short experience.  So, buy it with confidence.  As for details, here's the approach I took.

I hooked up one unit as instructed and updated firmware and measured my up and down speed.  I have a real basic internet speed so I know this unit is capable of doing more.  I used the same speedtest off the web for all my tests for consistency.  In general, I found this unit to be as fast as my old (read, real old) unit in the same room and the room next door.  Two rooms down, this unit is not strong as a dedicated router and speeds began to drop.  So, I added the second unit in the basement (I couldn't tell much difference between ethernet backhaul versus wifi but I think that has a lot to do with my basic internet package from my ISP.  I anticipate better results when I upgrade).  My third and final unit I felt wasn't even necessary.  Even the basement unit provided sufficient coverage in my upstairs bedroom which never worked with my single router.  I had three so I went ahead and put it in one of the bedrooms upstairs.

The app is good, you need a cloud id.  YouTube does a good job of all functions so all good.  Any questions, ask away.  Overall, a great buy so far.  Fingers crossed and I hope I don't have to come back and update my review (in a negative direction).
title: Cautiously optimistic
